answer_summary.reasoning: sp-hybridised cyclo[n]carbon rings carry two orthogonal cyclic pi systems with n pi electrons each. C18: 18 = 4*4+2 in both systems (2 aromatic). C16: 16 = 4*4 in both systems (2 anti-aromatic). C13: odd ring forces open shells (13 electrons per spin class is odd); triplet 3C13 delocalises 12 of 13 unpaired-spin electrons in the singly occupied system, 12 = 4*3 (1 anti-aromatic), while the 13-electron paired system is an open shell (neither); singlet 1C13 leaves the second system non-conjugated (lone pair orthogonal to cyclic pi), so both systems are neither aromatic nor anti-aromatic.

assumptions: Standard textbook model of cyclo[n]carbons: every ring carbon is sp-hybridised and supports two orthogonal cyclic pi systems (in-plane and out-of-plane), each receiving one pi electron per ring carbon.
Hueckel's rule applied per cyclic conjugated pi loop: aromatic iff electron count = 4k+2, anti-aromatic iff = 4k (closed-shell loops).

For odd C13 the two orthogonal systems cannot both be closed shells; the problem-given spin isomers carry one fully occupied (13 paired electrons) and one singly occupied (13 unpaired-spin electrons) pi system.

3C13 (S=1): Hund's rule separates the two frontier electrons into different MOs, so 12 of 13 unpaired-spin electrons count toward cyclic delocalisation; 13-electron loops are open shells (13 is neither 4k nor 4k+2).
1C13 (S=0): frontier electrons pair up, depopulating the second cyclic loop (lone pair orthogonal to cyclic pi conjugation), so no second aromatic/anti-aromatic system exists.
Counts of 'distinct pi systems' are per orthogonal cyclic conjugated loop, the standard cyclocarbon counting.
